thread.title: The Fall Of 2 Dividend Champions - Altria Group, Inc. (NYSE:MO)

author: Stefan Redlich
title: The Fall Of 2 Dividend Champions - Altria Group, Inc. (NYSE:MO)
text:
Dividend investors hungry for yield are currently spoilt for choice. Not too long ago, it was difficult to find solid companies paying 3% to 3.5% and above as valuations on traditional dividend friendly industries such as consumer staples, utilities, tobacco, and telecoms have been elevated.
As multiples started to compress, even almighty dividend stocks such as Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ) and 3M ( MMM ) have almost reached that illustrious 3% yield barrier.
In the consumer staples universe, dividend aristocrats Procter & Gamble ( PG ), Coca-Cola ( KO ), PepsiCo ( PEP ) are all substantially yielding above 3% and almost 4% in the case of the former.
In the utility sector yields for Dominion Energy ( D ), Southern Company ( SO ), and Duke (NYSE: DUK ) are currently between 4.6% and 5.3%.
In the tobacco sector, almighty Altria ( MO ) has seen a sharp fall from almost $78 down to $54 and is yielding above 5%. Altria's former parent, Philip Morris (NYSE: PM ), is yielding even more at 5.2%.
Finally, the telecom sector with heavyweights Verizon ( VZ ) and AT&T ( T ) is boasting the highest yields of 5.1% and a whopping 6.3%.
Naturally, higher yield comes with higher risk. In this article, we will scrutinize the investment thesis for Altria and AT&T, two of my largest portfolio positions and both deep in the red. Is this the right time to buy even more or are these stocks trapped in a downward spiral with no end in sight?
What is going on at AT&T?
Source: AT&T Investor Relations
In a nutshell, a lot and probably too much to handle at once:
AT&T is trapped in a costly trial over its acquisition with Time Warner ( TWX ) where the outcome is unknown and could result in even bigger movements of the stock. Its already sky-high debt level will reach astronomic heights should that deal go through, and with interest rates on the rise, it becomes more and more costly for the telecom giant to service its debt (with or without Time Warner). Apart from the huge boost from the tax reform the company's business is only growing marginally and faces heavy competition from both Sprint (NYSE: S ) and T-Mobile ( TMUS ) but also increasingly from content providers such as Netflix ( NFLX ) or Apple ( AAPL ). Let's dig deeper now!
In terms of business performance, the company completely missed estimates for the first quarter, but the revenue miss was certainly the most disappointing part both in terms of magnitude ($1.27B), but even more in terms of Y/Y performance (-3.4%).
T Revenue (Annual) data by YCharts
That chart shows that AT&T has grown its revenues over the last 10 years by around $30B. However, most of that originates from the costly DirecTV deal. Organically, growth has been marginal at best. AT&T's customer base is growing strongly, but that comes at the expense of losing more valuable customers (at least right now) in its more profitable Entertainment business segment. Cord-cutting is a major issue for the company. It lost 187,000 subscribers in the past quarter in linear video. And although it added almost twice as many in the OTT video segment (+312,000), that growth was not enough to offset the lost margin.
Over the last couple of quarters, the stock price movement is heavily characterized by declining sales and profits in the company's Entertainment business. If customers switch from paying $100 per month for cable to $30 per month for DirecTV and its services, AT&T will have to acquire a lot more customers in the lower margin business to offset the decline in the other. A net total of 125,000 subs across linear and OTT video is simply not enough to grow the top line. However, compared to Q1/2017, the performance is much better. Back then, AT&T lost 233,000 linear video subscribers and only added 72,000 OTT video subscribers, resulting in a net loss of 161,000 subs. As a result, compared to the previous year's quarter, the company improved by 286,000 subs. Still, this was not enough to post growth or at least keep the group's revenue stable. With the next generation DirecTV NOW platform to be launched this quarter, the fiscal Q2 report should paint a different picture and actually show many more new OTT video subscribers.
As a dividend investor, you may think that these are temporary problems as the company transforms itself into a leading content provider which allows to bundle services and generate more value by customer. This is certainly the long-term strategy, but high debt load and a deteriorating business may pose a risk to the dividend. In that case, it would not be worth to invest at a 6% yield if the dividend is at risk of not being raised or even worse being cut.
For Q1, the FCF dividend payout ratio stood at 108%, or to put differently, the company was not able to fully fund its dividend by organic free cash flow. That is a pretty strong argument against the stock, but digging deeper, at least for Q1, the situation is by far not as critical as it appears. Management said that,
The first quarter is traditionally our lowest free cash flow quarter and this year is no different. Several items impacted free cash flow, including our annual employee bonus program, a larger than usual handset payment from the very strong gross add and upgrade performance during the light holiday season in the fourth quarter and continuing into the first quarter.
We also had unreimbursed FirstNet expenditures in this quarter.
Source: Q1/2018 Earnings Call
What's more, on top of that, management reiterated full-year free cash flow guidance of $21B. But wait! Given that FCF only came in at around $3B in Q1, this would imply $6B FCF on average for each of the three remaining quarters. Should that happen, the payout ratio would only be around 60% and the dividend as safe as ever. However, $6B FCF by quarter is a big number. In 2017, AT&T recorded around $4.8B in FCF over the three remaining quarters. An increase to $6B represents 25% more FCF, which is certainly a high target. If the company succeeds in meeting that target (a big thanks to the tax reform here), then the current stock price is a fantastic buying opportunity . If it does not succeed and only achieves its 2017 levels, then the dividend would still be safe with a payout ratio of around 74%, but management would have lost about all remaining credibility, and the stock would likely tank further.
I have been very bullish on the company's future all the time (otherwise, it would not be my biggest position in terms of cost basis), but as the company has failed to deliver, I have become a little bit more cautious, primarily due to the fact that the company's cash flow generation targets are very ambitious. At this stage, I am HOLDING my position waiting for AT&T's Q2 report for which FCF generation will be key to me. AT&T has substantially underperformed the market for at least two decades, and I see no reason for that trend to change. Still, if you are on the hunt for dividend income, this stock represents the highest-yielding opportunity in the mega-cap segment. A lot of negativity has been priced into the stock, but with the Time Warner trial still being anyone's guess, a high degree of uncertainty will likely accompany the stock as this year unfolds.
What is going on at Altria? For a stock that outperformed the general market over vast stretches of time, the fall of Altria's stock is even worse than what AT&T is experiencing.
The stock is currently trading a whopping 29% below its 52-week high and yielding a monstrous 5.1%.
MO data by YCharts
For only the second time over a 5-year period, investors have been worse off investing in Altria than into the broad S&P 500 ( SPY ) but have still been doing reasonably well. For Altria's 2017 investors, the situation looks very bleak right now as the stock is a full 35pp behind the broad market.
MO data by YCharts
So, what is driving this and should dividend investors be worried?
First and foremost, Altria is in a very difficult situation right now. As the decline of cigarette volumes accelerated, which cannot be offset by growing volumes of the non-smokeable segment questions and doubts about Altria's future are cast. IQOS, which is expected to act as the savior to that deteriorating trend, has still not been approved by the FDA for the U.S., and with IQOS growth slowing down at Philip Morris, more uncertainty is created as regards the true business potential for IQOS.
Altria's stock has already experienced three sharp sell-offs over the last 52 weeks: first, when the FDA made its surprising 2017 summer statement, second, when the treasury yield hovered around the 3% mark for the first time in early-to-mid April and third when Philip Morris tanked more than 10% the day it released its Q1/2018 earnings.
When Altria released its own earnings, the stock dipped a bit further despite the company beating estimates both on the top and bottom line. At first glance, the results were actually surprisingly good with net revenue growing by 1.8% and net income jumping 35% (mostly driven by the tax reform). The company also reaffirmed its full-year EPS guidance. That's it as far as the positives are concerned.
On the flip side, the real dealbreaker with Altria is volumes. Altria's biggest segment, "smokeable products", has seen an alarming 4.2% decline in cigarette shipment volume. Not only did volume fell but Altria's top-selling Marlboro brand also lost 0.5 percentage points in market share. Thanks to Altria's pricing power, net revenues only declined by 0.8% for the segment and even posted a 0.4% gain if deducting excise taxes. However, due to favorable inventory movements, the 4.2% volume decline is understating the actual trend. In its press statement, the company mentions:
When adjusted for trade inventory movements, smokeable products segment domestic cigarette shipment volume decreased by an estimated 7%
Source: Altria Q1/2018 Press Release
That is a 7% decline in Altria's most important and profitable business segment, and pricing power will not be able to offset these losses forever as it has done for so many years in the past. Prices for cigarette packs have risen substantially over the last decade, and while there are still many states where a pack costs below $7 several states already have double-digit per pack prices. California has seen the strongest rise in cigarette prices over the last year (from $7.16 to $10.51) as the state imposed an extra $2 per pack excise tax. Overall, there is still room for further price hikes, but with volumes showing no signs to stop their decline, the discrepancy between the two factors will continue to widen.
In "smokeless products", overall volumes stagnated with -0.1% percentage change, but revenues grew by around 13%, and operating income jumped by a staggering 27%. Retail share for that segment remained virtually unchanged, but the discrepancy between volumes and operating income is surprising. Altria mentions that the strong operating metrics are " primarily driven by the impact the 2017 voluntary recall and higher pricing had " but unfortunately does not break down these two effects. We need to strongly monitor these developments over the next couple of quarters before ringing any alarm bells here. At the very least, though, with volumes stagnating, it should be safe to assume that the bottom line will not grow more than single digits from hereon as the pricing power Altria has with Copenhagen and Skoal is certainly weaker than Marlboro's.
Listening to the earnings call, management did not reveal any sense of concern regarding these figures, instead Marty Barrington stated that,
Altria is off to a fast start to the strong year of EPS growth to which we've guided
Source: Altria Q1/2018 Earnings Call
That is certainly true but, predominantly, the result of the tax reform, which also allowed for an out-of-cycle 6% dividend hike in March . Altria's vapor segment is not really growing strong at this stage, but with volumes declining rapidly for traditional cigarettes, the company faces a very challenging situation.
On the volume side, Altria's management, despite not releasing specific guidance here, is confident that they expect the rate of the declines to moderate throughout 2018, but what is driving this confidence, apart from California's special excise tax in 2017 affecting Y/Y comparisons, is unclear. Investors can either believe Altria's word here which is based on sound and sophisticated models or simply confront themselves with a brutal reality check which does not really give a lot of optimism that with regulatory pressures mounting every day volume declines will slow down. The truth probably lies in between.
It is very difficult to judge whether management is still on top of its business or trapped in a disrupting business environment where its top line is slowly breaking away as innovative new products are not reaping the expected rewards. Innovation across vapor-based products, gaining FDA approval while still managing to generate as much revenue as possible from its Marlboro cash cow.
Altria has been in difficult situations before. Being a major player in the arguably most regulated and most scrutinized industry, uncertainty and challenges are part of Altria's bloodline. However, simply assuming that since management was able to mitigate the impact from the Master Tobacco Settlement Agreement and all the regulatory hurdles it has been confronted with over time such as rising taxes, commercial restrictions, shock picture on packs and so on, it can do the same again is lacking context and could be a classic case of confirmation bias . The situation is completely different. Back then, cigarette prices have been very low, and smoker rates still comparatively high. With prices increasing substantially and the number of smokers declining significantly, the room for maneuver is much smaller. Also, if, on the one hand, your traditional cash cows are receiving less and less demand and new products are not receiving as much adoption as expected the business will certainly dry out. Sooner or later, the world will turn tobacco-free, and if Altria wants to remain a major player here, it needs to be more aggressive now.
At this stage, Altria's yield looks enticing, but with the challenges for the company mounting every day, Altria's future gets more and more uncertain. I am not heralding the demise of Altria here, but investors should not turn a blind eye and accept that the challenges the company is facing right now are fundamentally different to those of the past and can endanger the company's business model.
I remain LONG on the stock but have slightly trimmed my holdings (to reduce risk exposure despite taking some losses) as the outlook is very unclear to me. At this stage, I would love to add to the stock, but with so much change happening in the industry, which I admittedly have not taken seriously enough before, management needs to outline its strategy how it intends to deal with this situation in case its current strategy does not pay off.
Investor takeaway Both stocks have been beaten down, and both stocks are sporting juicy yields. For both stocks, the high yield comes with a high degree of risk, but the situation is much different.
For Altria, the market has not only started to price in a high degree of uncertainty but also potentially sees the company's business model at risk. Investing in the tobacco industry which is heavily regulated and only one FDA announcement away from collapsing 20% any day has always been risky . With business fundamentals deteriorating and management not giving clear evidence as to how it expects the situation to change, the stock has no real positive catalyst here. The next 5 years will be key to Altria's future. It needs to diversify into new products or even into a new industry, as it did with its 11% stake in Anheuser-Busch InBev ( BUD ), as long as its "smokeable segment" is still generating lots of revenue and income.
In the case of AT&T, the fundamentals are not as bad as the yield would imply. It is true that it is losing customers from cutting the cord and is boasting a very high debt level, but it also has a lot of future catalysts, most notably, 5G and the ever increasing internet usage. Its overall customer base is not breaking away but increasing by hundreds of thousands of customers. If that potential starts to get monetized via cross-selling and with the integration of Time Warner, in case it gets approved, business fundamentals will improve substantially.
Falling dividend champions could be life-time opportunities for investors or real portfolio breakers . I will continue to hold my investments, drip the dividend income, and monitor how things progress in the second quarter. It is much too early to claim that the two companies are at the crossroads, but in both cases, the higher yield reflects the higher risk associated with both stocks.
What do you think about these two companies? Are you investing more on recent price weakness, holding your position or selling out and moving on to other investments?
